title: Chapter 62 – Taking the Cradle
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The Court's rider does not dismount.

He sits his gray horse in the gatehouse yard with the reins in one gloved hand and a scroll case in the other, and he waits while Elder Zhong comes out, bows, takes the case, and writes the hour and the rider's seal number in the Garden ledger. It is the first thing Zhong has entered in that ledger that is not a harvest. He writes slowly. The rider watches him do it, then turns his horse and goes back down the road at a walk, as if there were nothing in the case that could not wait for a clerk's handwriting.

Jian sees all of it from the forge steps, with a bowl of millet going cold on his knee.

Zhong carries the case to the study himself. It is a short walk, and the old man takes it as if the case weighed a great deal more than paper. By the time Jian follows, his father has already read the letter twice.

"Trust inspectors," says Wenyuan. He sets the sheet on the table and smooths it flat with his bandaged hand. "The Court's Garden Office. They arrive at noon tomorrow. They will survey the Orchard, count the Wardens, record every structure, and place a Court seal on any chamber they judge unsafe, to be held until the trust is reviewed." He looks up. "It is courteous of them to warn us. It is also an order."

"How many?" asks Jian.

"Eight. A deputy, five clerks, two Qi Refining guards." Wenyuan taps the last line. "The deputy is a man named Dou. Cheng Yun's office, but not Cheng Yun."

A deputy, not an inspector, thinks Jian. Someone who writes down what he sees and sends it on.

"Every structure," he says.

"Every structure." His father is watching him now, the way he has watched him since the siege, with a care that has not yet decided whether it is pride or worry. "Jian. Is there anything in that Orchard the Court should not find?"

There are several answers. Most are lies. One is true, and not complete.

"There is a plate on the terrace," says Jian. "Beside the pool. It is round, and broken at one edge, and it does not open for anyone."

"It opened for you."

"Once. For my hand." He says it carefully, because it is the only part he can say. "I do not think it will open for theirs."

Wenyuan is silent for a moment. Then he nods, once, and folds the letter along its old creases.

"Then let them look at it," he says. "A door that opens for no one is only a stone."

It is exactly the right answer, and Jian is grateful for it, and he does not trust it to last past noon tomorrow.

He goes out into the yard. The morning is cold and bright. Over the wall, the quarry road runs gray between the pines, and beyond the quarry is the east wall, and behind the east wall, under a hill that the Court now holds in trust, is a round room with a thing in it that was cut to fit a hand.

A Court seal, he thinks. Wax on the plate. A guard on the terrace. A ten-year review.

He does the arithmetic as he would for a batch of pills. The cradle cannot be put back, the wall said, once it is taken. It does not say it cannot be taken. If the inspectors seal that chamber, the cradle becomes the Court's to find, to open, or to wait on for ten years while Shen Wuye decides what a boy's handprint means. If Jian takes it tonight, he carries it to the Outer Court himself, in seven months, past a lock he has not yet seen.

Do not let them have it, wrote Feng. Say it is a pill.

Pebble is asleep in the crook of his arm, curled into a ball the size of a loaf, her scales dull and her breath slow. She has been sleeping for most of the autumn. When he lifts his hand to her back, one dark eye opens a crack.

Tonight, he thinks.

Tonight, she agrees, from somewhere very far down in a dream, and closes the eye.

* * *

The hill has a night routine now, and he has learned it.

Two guards at the quarry gate, changing at the third watch. Wenshi's lantern on the terrace wall, burning low. Zhong in the gatehouse, awake at all hours, writing names in a ledger that no longer has anything to say. Jian waits in the dark of the forge yard until the lantern bell rings the hour, and then he does a thing he has practiced since the summer and never once in earnest.

He sets his feet. He lets the Veil Step run.

His mother taught it to him on a summer evening, in the ash-gray light behind the granary, one palm on his shoulder to feel the Qi move. It is a Yellow technique, a rogue cultivator's trick, and it is not a Veil in the ordinary sense. It does not hide him. It lets him move between the places where people look. It costs twice the Qi it should, and it lasts only as long as a man can hold his breath, and when it ends it ends all at once.

Jian counts. One. Two. He crosses the yard in the gap between the lantern's swing and the guard's turned shoulder. Seven. Eight. He is at the quarry gate. Eleven. He passes the sentry's left elbow, close enough to smell the wet wool of his cloak, and the man does not turn his head.

Fourteen. The step breaks. His Qi gutters, hard, like a flame in a draft. He puts his back against a pine and breathes through his teeth until the shaking in his hands stops.

That is the price, he thinks. Twice the Qi, and a minute you cannot spend twice.

You are loud, says Pebble, drowsily. But not to them.

Thank you.

It was not a compliment.

The quarry is a bowl of black stone under a pale moon. The east wall rises at the far side, and in it, where a seam was once wrenched open by force and later closed by a patient hand, there is a plain door of old planks, a Lin lock, and a hanging tag that reads Garden: by leave of the Patriarch. Wenyuan gave him the key at the evening meal without a word. He has not asked since.

The door opens on the cool, damp smell of living things.

The Orchard is quieter than it was. The red haze that once lay over it is gone, and the beds have drunk back what was taken, and the long rows of old trees stand in the dark with their branches drawn in, like sleepers. The pool glows at the heart of the terrace. A deep, soft, living green. Around it, in their ring, stand the eleven Wardens, tall figures of moss and iron-gray stone, motionless, waiting. When Jian walks past the nearest, its head turns, very slowly, and follows him as far as the steps.

It does nothing else. It has learned his hands.

The plate lies in the paving where he left it, round and pale and broken at one edge. He kneels. He puts his right palm to it, and a thread of Qi, the thin cold one, goes down into the stone.

The plate sighs. A seam of silver light runs across it, and the central slab drops away, and the stair is there again, black and narrow, going down.

He picks up his lantern.

Forty, he thinks. Forty steps. And one lock at the bottom of someone else's forty.

He counts them down.

* * *

The chamber is as he left it.

It is a round room, no wider than the forge, with a floor of pale tile and a ceiling that curves in like the inside of a bowl. There is nothing on the walls but the inscription, three lines in a hand he can almost read. There is a low pedestal at the center. On the pedestal, set into a shallow cup of silver metal, is the cradle.

It is smaller than he remembers. A ring of glassy studs, a slender curved neck, a bowl the color of old pewter. Under the lantern light it looks like a thing a careful man might set on a shelf. Only the stud that glowed when he left is glowing still, a faint steady blue, like the tip of a coal.

He has seen this before, in a white room, under a lamp, on a night when he had other things to be afraid of. He does not let himself linger on that. He has seven hours until dawn and a plan, and the plan begins with a question.

Scan Structure, he thinks, and does not say aloud.

```
[SCAN STRUCTURE — Level 3]
Target: SCANNER COIL (primary), ARK-7
Cost: 12 CE
Confirm? [Y/N]
```

Yes.

```
[CE 94 -> 82]
Structure resolved.
Mounting collar: 7-lobed, KEYED. Requires external dock.
Dock present in this chamber: NO.
Tether: 1 (to pedestal cup). Severable.
Pedestal cup is NOT the dock. Cup is a cradle only.
Dock class: wall-mounted lock, keyed to collar.
Reference dock: not in scan range.
Seal: chamber-bound. Severing tether BREAKS seal.
Consequence (projected): chamber inner stair will close.
Consequence (projected): reservoir draw will drop on removal.
Integration: NOT required for transport.
```

He reads it twice.

Wall-mounted lock, he thinks. Keyed to the collar.

He cannot verify it. The panel has told him so; the reference dock is outside its range. But a boy at the Outer Court has been standing in front of a lock at the fortieth step for half a year, and the cradle is a thing that needs a lock. It is not proof. It is the shape of a piece, held up against the shape of a hole he has not yet seen.

Say it is a pill, thinks Jian. Feng. What did you find on that stair?

He turns the lantern on the walls and reads the inscription once more. What you take from this room, you will not be able to put back. It has said the same three lines in the same stone for a very long time. It has been telling the truth the entire time.

What does the pool lose, if I take it? he asks Pebble.

She has climbed down off his shoulder onto the tile, and she is standing with her small clawed forepaws on the edge of the pedestal, looking up at the cradle. Her scales catch the blue of the stud, and for a breath they are almost bright.

A little, she says. The garden is leaning on it. Not hard. Like a hand on a table. If the hand goes, the table will shake.

How much?

I do not know numbers. A pause. A tenth. It might be a tenth.

A tenth of the reservoir's draw. A tenth of the herb beds' growth, over a season, over a year, over every year that three hundred and ninety-one people eat from it by need. The Arbiter ruled that the Garden could keep a clan alive but not a Sect. Jian has been counting that line since the day he heard it. A tenth is not much. It is a family's winter ration, a handful of sick, a child's pills.

I am about to take from my own clan to feed myself, he thinks, flatly. It is better that I say it plainly.

Yes, says Pebble.

And if I leave it?

Then men with wax come, and they put it in a box. She considers. I think the cradle would be sad in a box.

He almost laughs. It comes out as a cough.

There are two ledgers in his head, and neither one is clean. He writes down what leaving it costs: the Court's seal, the Court's guards, the Court's patience, ten years of a thing he is meant to carry kept from his hand. He writes down what taking it costs: a tenth of the clan's winter, and a stair that will not open again. Then he does what he has always done with a ledger he does not like. He looks for what he can do to the numbers.

Pebble. Could the Wardens make up a tenth?

Slowly. She tilts her head. If they were told to. If someone fed the beds by hand, for a season, like the old woman with the water.

Hu, thinks Jian. And Mother. And the herb rotation Wenqing keeps. He will not be able to tell them why. He will only be able to ask them to be a little more careful with a garden that has begun to tire, and hope that they put it down to autumn.

It is not enough. It is not nothing.

He steps up to the pedestal. Under the lantern, the cradle pulses once, softly, like a sleeper turning in a dream.

He takes Ke Tian's pouch from under his tunic.

It is a plain gray bag, tied at the mouth with a cord of braided hair, a Yellow-tier storage pouch with a blood-key that he stripped off with a four-point Separation in the autumn, on a night he does not think about. It holds a little over two cubic meters of dead matter. It will hold a bowl of pewter and a neck of glass. It will not hold anything that breathes.

He ties it open. He sets it beneath the cradle's silver cup, his left hand steadying the lip, and with his right, very gently, he lifts the thing out of its cradle.

```
[TETHER SEVERED]
Chamber seal: BROKEN.
Inner stair: CLOSING.
Reservoir draw: -9%.
Cradle status: DORMANT. Transport: PERMITTED.
Integration: NOT initiated.
```

The cradle weighs nothing. It weighs about as much as an empty cup. It slides into the mouth of the pouch with a soft, dry whisper, and the pouch's cord draws tight on its own.

Then the floor moves.

It is a small movement, a shiver in the tile, a grinding from far overhead. The lantern flame bends sideways. Pebble's claws find his ankle, and the walls, the plain curved walls with their three lines of script, begin very slowly to settle, as if the whole room were exhaling.

Up, says Pebble. Up. Now.

He runs.

* * *

Forty steps.

They are shorter on the way up. He does not understand it, and he has no time to ask. He takes them two at a time with the lantern bobbing wildly in his left hand and the pouch banging against his ribs, and under his feet the stair is folding, one tread sliding flat beneath the next, a long stone hand closing slowly on itself. Thirty-one. Thirty. The dust comes down in sheets. Twenty. A crack runs up the wall beside his shoulder and stops. Fourteen.

His Qi is almost empty. He has nothing left to run on but fear and the memory of the rhythm. Ten.

At the top, the plate above him is already sealing, the broken edge knitting together with a thread of silver, the slab sliding back toward its seat. He has a moment, a single breath, in which the gap is a hand's width, then two fingers. He throws the lantern through it. Then Pebble. Then his own arm, to the shoulder, and he hauls himself up and out onto the paving with the stone grinding at the hem of his tunic.

The plate shuts.

It shuts with a soft, final sound, like a book closed on a name. A thin line of silver light runs round the rim, and goes out.

He lies on his back on the terrace stones, with the pouch crushed against his chest and his lungs working like bellows. Above him, through the black branches of the old trees, the stars are very cold and very clear.

You are not dead, says Pebble, with the quiet satisfaction of someone confirming a calculation.

No.

Good. She has crawled onto his stomach and settled there. I did not like that.

Neither did I.

He turns his head, slowly. The pool has dimmed. It is only a shade; he would not have noticed, a day ago. The deep, soft green is a little less deep. Around the ring, the Wardens have moved, in the time it took him to run, in perfect unison, with a sound like a long stone breath. All eleven of them are bowing. Not to the pool. Not to the plate.

Toward him.

He lies very still. A moss-grown head the size of a barrel inclines in the dark, and holds, and slowly lifts again, and the ring goes back to stillness as if nothing had passed.

They know it left, says Pebble. They are not angry. They are... I think it is something like sorry.

For what?

For the table.

He sits up. His hands are shaking again. He presses them hard against his knees, and then he sees that there is someone on the terrace steps.

Old Hu is sitting on the top step with a blanket round his shoulders and his one hand in his lap. The other sleeve is pinned to his chest. There is a clay pot of tea by his foot and, beside it, a second cup, upside-down, as if he had meant to pour it and had thought better.

He has been there for some time. The pot is cold.

Jian opens his mouth.

"The pool dimmed," says Hu. His voice is a rasp. He is looking at the water, not at the boy. "About an hour ago. A tenth, no more. I have watched it every night since the siege, and it has not shifted a hair in that time." A pause. "I do not know what it means."

"Hu," says Jian.

"I will be here until the sun is up." The old man does not turn. "The Wardens do not like to be alone with the beds. I find it settles them." He pulls the blanket higher. "You should go to bed. Your mother will notice the dust on your cloak. Brush it before you go in."

He does not ask.

It is the kindest thing anyone has done for Jian in a year, and he cannot say so. He gets to his feet. He brushes the dust from his cloak and the stone from his sleeves, and he stands there a moment longer, with a hundred words in his throat and a gray pouch tied against his ribs that he is forbidden to explain.

"Thank you," he says, finally.

"For what?" says Hu. "I have been sitting here all night with a pot of tea." He reaches down and turns the second cup right-side up with two fingers. "Go on."

* * *

The inspectors arrive at noon, exactly, in two covered carts and a gray mule's patience.

There are eight of them, as promised, and they dismount at the gatehouse in the order of their rank. First the two guards, in plain brown tunics with the Court's cloud-stitch at the collar. Then five clerks with measuring cords, folding boards, ink blocks and rolls of paper. Last, a lean, careful man in a short gray robe with a wooden tally-stick at his belt, who looks round the yard as if he were already writing it.

"Deputy Dou, of the Garden Office," he says to Wenyuan, and bows exactly the required depth. "I regret the intrusion, Patriarch. My orders are specific. We will be brief."

They are not brief. They are thorough.

By the second hour they have paced the quarry bowl and measured it. By the third they have mapped the Orchard from the east door to the pool, and counted the Wardens, and entered the number in four hands: eleven. They have refused tea. They have refused, politely, the offer of an escort, and have walked every aisle of the beds with Zhong's ledger open under a clerk's arm, matching each name in the book to a root in the ground. They do not touch anything. They write everything down.

Jian stands with the clan, in the second row, among the children and the women, in a plain gray tunic, with his hands folded and his eyes on his feet. Pebble is not on his shoulder. She is in the forge, asleep in a basket, which Hu has said is a thing a spirit beast does in winter. Ke Tian's pouch is under his tunic. It has been there all night, and all morning, and he has not moved it once.

If he asks me to empty my sleeves, thinks Jian, I will say it is a pill.

It is a stupid thought. He holds onto it anyway.

The deputy reaches the terrace in the middle of the afternoon.

He stands at the head of the steps for a while, looking down at the pool, with the green light moving on his lean face. The Wardens do not stir. He writes a line. Then he walks, without hurry, to the pale round plate in the paving, and crouches, and lays two fingers flat against the stone.

Nothing happens.

He tries three more spots on its face. He tries its broken edge. He asks, politely, if the Patriarch will place his hand. Wenyuan does, with a straight back and the bandage tucked behind him, and the stone gives nothing. Wenqing tries, because she is clan, and she is the nearest. Then Wenshi, who is Qi Refining seven and has a hand like a shovel. Then, at last, almost reluctantly, one of the Court guards, a young man with a scarred chin who sets his palm to the plate and presses until the cords stand out in his arm.

It is as dead as a cobble.

"A dead disc," says the guard. He straightens. "Rank one at best, Deputy. There is no Qi in it. Not a thread."

"Is there not?" says Dou.

He is still crouched. He has taken a small brush from his sleeve, and he is touching it, lightly, to a patch of paving a handspan from the plate's rim, where the stone has taken a very faint polish, as if it had once held the warmth of a hand.

Jian's stomach turns over.

He has not thought of the print.

It is nothing. It is a smudge of pale silver in the gray, the size of a small child's palm, with the five short fingers a little spread. It was not there yesterday. It should not be there now: he put his hand to the stone in the dark and the stone drank it, and went cold. He sees now that it has not drunk all of it. It left the outline, like frost on a window, a ghost of the thing that had opened the door.

Dou takes a clean sheet from his folding board. He sketches it, in three swift lines, and a fourth for the thumb. He adds the measurements in a small, tidy hand: Palm: 8.5 cm. Fingers: 6. Left or right: right. Age: child, under twelve. He looks at the sketch for a long moment, and then, not at the Patriarch, not at the guards, not at Zhong or at Wenshi, but at the second row of the clan, where the children stand, he lets his eyes travel once along the line of small gray tunics, without stopping on any one of them.

Then he rolls the sketch in a tube of oiled paper, and seals the end with a thumb of red wax.

"A curiosity," he says, to no one. "The Arbiter will want to see it."

He hands the tube to a rider. The rider is already mounted, on a long-legged gray horse, with his reins in one gloved hand, and he takes it without a word and turns toward the road.

Jian watches the dust rise behind him until the road bends.

Six days, he thinks. Perhaps five, if the horse is good. Five days for a child's handprint to reach Shen Wuye's desk, in a tube of oiled paper, under a seal that any clerk could break.

And under his tunic, against his ribs, quite still, the cradle gives a long slow pulse, as if it, too, were listening.
